title: DAVID WALKED TOWARD GOLIATH WITH FIVE STONES—AND REFUSED SAUL’S ARMOR
paragraphs: DAVID WALKED TOWARD GOLIATH WITH FIVE STONES—AND REFUSED SAUL’S ARMOR
The giant was covered in bronze. David carried a sling. But the most dangerous thing on that battlefield was not what David held in his hand—it was Who David knew was fighting the battle.
There is a moment in the story of David and Goliath that we often rush past.
We remember the stone.
We remember the sling.
We remember the giant crashing to the earth.
But before David ever picked up those five smooth stones, something quieter happened.
Something deeply uncomfortable.
David took off the armor.
King Saul had dressed him for battle.
Helmet.
Armor.
Sword.
Everything a warrior was supposed to wear.
Everything that looked responsible.
Everything that made sense to frightened human eyes.
And David tried to walk.
Then he stopped.
Because sometimes the first act of faith is not picking something up.
Sometimes it is finally having the courage to take something off.
The Hebrew text of 1 Samuel 17:39 preserves David’s words:
“לֹא אוּכַל לָלֶכֶת בָּאֵלֶּה כִּי לֹא נִסִּיתִי”
Lo ukhal lalekhet ba'elleh, ki lo nissiti.
In context:
“I cannot go with these, because I have not tested them.”
Then Scripture says:
“וַיְסִרֵם דָּוִד מֵעָלָיו”
Vayesirem David me'alav.
David removed them from himself.
That sentence is easy to read.
Living it is harder.
Because Saul's armor was not necessarily bad armor.
It simply was not David's tested equipment.
And there are things in your life that may not be sinful in themselves, yet they become dangerous when you begin trusting them more than you trust God.
Someone else's image.
Someone else's calling.
Someone else's personality.
Someone else's success.
Someone else's way of praying.
Someone else's ministry.
Someone else's approval.
Someone else's definition of what a victorious Christian is supposed to look like.
You can spend years trying to walk in armor God never trained you to wear.
And perhaps that is why you are exhausted.
Not because God abandoned you.
Maybe you have been trying to fight tomorrow's battle dressed in somebody else's expectations.
David took Saul's armor off.
Then he walked toward the water.
Scripture says:
“וַיִּבְחַר־לוֹ חֲמִשָּׁה חַלֻּקֵי־אֲבָנִים מִן־הַנַּחַל”
He chose for himself five smooth stones from the brook.
Five.
Not because Scripture secretly assigns each stone a mystical meaning.
The Bible does not tell us that one stone represented faith, another courage, another prayer, another obedience, and another grace.
Those can make memorable sermon illustrations, but they should not be confused with what the biblical text actually says.
Scripture simply tells us David chose five smooth stones.
And there is something even more beautiful than inventing symbolism.
David came carrying ordinary things into an impossible situation while trusting an extraordinary God.
A shepherd's staff.
A pouch.
A sling.
Five stones.
That was what people could see.
What they could not see was everything God had already done in the wilderness.
David had been keeping sheep when nobody thought he mattered.
He had faced the lion.
He had faced the bear.
He had learned what deliverance felt like before there was an audience to applaud him.
That matters.
Because sometimes God prepares His servants where nobody is watching.
The private battle.
The lonely prayer.
The night you cried and still opened your Bible the next morning.
The temptation nobody knew you resisted.
The season when nobody congratulated you for remaining faithful.
The forgiveness you gave while your heart was still bleeding.
The worship whispered from a room where you felt forgotten.
You called it obscurity.
God may have been calling it training.
David had already told Saul that the LORD who delivered him from the lion and the bear would deliver him from the Philistine.
David's confidence was not positive thinking.
It had history behind it.
He remembered God.
And then the shepherd walked into the valley.
Try to see it.
Goliath is approaching with a shield-bearer ahead of him.
The Philistine warrior sees David and despises him.
He sees youth.
He sees vulnerability.
He sees a staff.
He does not see what David sees.
And perhaps that is where some of us have been losing battles before they even begin.
We have been staring at what the giant has instead of remembering Who God is.
Goliath has armor.
God is still God.
Goliath has a spear.
God is still God.
Goliath has experience.
God is still God.
Goliath is terrifying.
God is still God.
Your diagnosis may frighten you.
God is still God.
Your marriage may be hurting.
God is still God.
Your child may be wandering.
God is still God.
Your past may still whisper your name.
God is still God.
Your bank account may make you afraid to look.
God is still God.
Your addiction may have knocked you down again.
God is still God.
Your grief may make getting out of bed feel like warfare.
God is still God.
That does not mean every earthly story ends exactly the way we demand.
Biblical faith is not manipulating God into giving us our preferred outcome.
It means that even when the valley is real, the enemy is real, the pain is real, and tomorrow is uncertain, God remains God.
Then David speaks.
And suddenly the entire story changes.
Goliath had been talking about weapons.
David starts talking about God.
“You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin…”
Then comes the sentence that reveals why this shepherd boy is standing while trained soldiers are hiding.
David says he comes in the name of the LORD of hosts—the God of the armies of Israel.
And then:
“כִּי לַיהוָה הַמִּלְחָמָה”
Ki laYHWH hammilchamah.
For the battle belongs to the LORD.
There it is.
Not:
“The battle belongs to David.”
Not:
“I am stronger than you think.”
Not:
“Believe in yourself.”
Not:
“Manifest your victory.”
Not:
“You have a giant-killer hidden inside you.”
No.
The battle belongs to the LORD.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because the story of David and Goliath is not ultimately a motivational speech about discovering your inner champion.
It is a testimony to the living God who saves.
David explicitly says the coming victory will show the earth that there is a God in Israel and that the LORD does not save by sword and spear.
David's objective was larger than personal success.
He wanted God to be known.
And that exposes something in us.
How many times have we asked God for victory because we wanted to look victorious?
How many prayers were secretly asking:
“Lord, make them regret doubting me.”
“Lord, prove that I was right.”
“Lord, embarrass the people who embarrassed me.”
“Lord, make me successful enough that everyone who rejected me has to watch.”
But David's heart points somewhere higher.
Let the earth know there is a God.
That is different.
Faith does not merely ask, “How can I win?”
Faith asks:
“How can Christ be glorified through me?”
And then something happens that should change the way we picture David forever.
First Samuel 17:48 says that when Goliath moved forward, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him.
He ran.
Toward him.
The boy everybody underestimated ran toward the thing everybody feared.
Not because David believed stones were magical.
Not because David was incapable of fear.
Not because David had suddenly become physically greater than Goliath.
David had already settled the deepest question.
Who owns this battle?
The LORD.
And some of you reading this have spent years running in the opposite direction.
Running from confession.
Running from repentance.
Running from accountability.
Running from the conversation you know you need to have.
Running from church because somebody wounded you.
Running from Scripture because conviction became uncomfortable.
Running from prayer because silence made you wonder whether God was listening.
Running from Jesus because you are terrified of what surrender might cost.
You have changed relationships.
Changed churches.
Changed jobs.
Changed cities.
Changed passwords.
Changed appearances.
Changed your explanation.
But the wound came with you.
The shame came with you.
The secret came with you.
And eventually you discover something terrifying:
You can outrun people.
You cannot outrun your own soul.
Maybe your Goliath is not standing across a literal battlefield.
Maybe he is staring back from your mirror.
Maybe the giant has your voice.
Maybe it says:
“You'll never change.”
“You already ruined everything.”
“If people knew the real you, they would leave.”
“God must be tired of forgiving you.”
“You're too dirty now.”
“You're too compromised.”
“You knew better.”
“You promised God you would stop, and you went back.”
And this is where David's story must lead us beyond David.
Because David himself would eventually need grace.
The young shepherd who defeated Goliath would not live a spotless life.
Years later, King David would commit devastating sin involving Bathsheba and Uriah.
The giant-killer would become the man desperately crying for mercy.
And suddenly the Bible refuses to let us worship its human heroes.
David could defeat Goliath.
David could not become his own Savior.
Neither can you.
That is why this story ultimately leaves us hungry for someone greater than David.
Jesus Christ.
David entered a valley representing God's people against an enemy they feared.
But generations later, the Son of David entered a far deeper battle.
Christ did not merely confront a Philistine warrior.
He confronted sin.
Death.
Judgment.
The powers of darkness.
And unlike David, Jesus was without sin.
He did not need Saul's armor.
He did not need five stones.
He did not need an army to rescue Him.
He willingly went toward the cross.
People mocked Him.
Stripped Him.
Beat Him.
Rejected Him.
A crown of thorns was pressed onto His head.
Nails went through His hands and feet.
And to everyone watching, it looked like the enemy had won.
But Golgotha was not the collapse of God's rescue plan.
It was at the center of it.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And Jesus rose.
The grave did not get the final word.
Sin did not get the final word.
Satan did not get the final word.
Death did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
And this is where your story can change.
Not because you found the right five stones.
Not because you finally became strong enough.
Not because you learned how to imitate somebody else's armor.
But because the Gospel announces that sinners can be forgiven through Jesus Christ.
You do not need to pretend anymore.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the unbelief.
Bring Him the secret nobody knows.
Bring Him the religious performance.
Bring Him the nights you wish you could erase.
Repentance does not mean pretending your sin was small.
Grace means Christ is greater.
The cross does not tell you sin does not matter.
The cross tells you sin mattered so terribly that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners—and that His mercy reaches people who could never save themselves.
Maybe this article was supposed to be about David's five stones.
But perhaps God is pressing something else into your heart.
What armor are you still wearing?
What have you been trusting instead of Christ?
What identity are you terrified to remove?
What sin are you protecting because surrender feels too expensive?
What giant have you allowed to preach to you every morning?
And whose voice will have the final word?
Goliath's?
Your past's?
Your shame's?
The world's?
Or Jesus Christ's?
Be honest.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Send it to the believer who feels defeated.
Send it to the person who has wandered from God.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is simply about good people becoming better.
Send it to someone who needs to hear that Christianity is about sinners who need a Savior—and a Savior who is mighty to save.
Because there may come a morning when the giant sounds louder than your faith, and you will need to remember again:
כִּי לַיהוָה הַמִּלְחָמָה
Ki laYHWH hammilchamah.
The battle belongs to the LORD.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you return to Scripture, confronting you when you need conviction, or reminding you of Jesus when life becomes unbearably loud, stay close.
It is simply another way you can help Gospel Warrior keep putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it.
It is discipleship.
It is helping truth keep moving.
It is helping another exhausted believer encounter the Gospel at 2:00 in the morning.
It is helping another prodigal remember the Father's mercy.
It is helping another person hear the name of Jesus.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Do it because Jesus Christ is worthy of being known.
Do it because somebody's giant has been talking long enough.
Do it because somebody you know may be standing in a valley right now, convinced that the story is over.
David walked toward Goliath.
But David's greatest legacy was never a stone embedded in a giant's forehead.
David's story pointed beyond himself toward the greater Son of David.
Jesus.
The King who does not merely help broken people manage their scandals.
The King who forgives repentant sinners.
The King who restores.
The King who redeems.
The King who transforms.
The King who walked toward death itself—and walked out of the grave alive.
So take off the borrowed armor.
Stop pretending.
Stop letting shame write theology for you.
Turn from sin.
Come to Christ.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
And when the giant speaks again tomorrow, remember what David knew before the stone ever left the sling:
The size of the giant was never the final truth of the valley. The presence of God was.
And perhaps the thing you are most ashamed to place at the feet of Jesus will one day become the place where people see most clearly what His grace can rewrite.
